Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 48-year-old male here about trouble hearing. What's been going on?
Patient: It's my right ear. Everything sounds muffled, and it crept up slowly over about four months. I really noticed it after I got back from a trip overseas.
Doctor: Where did you travel?
Patient: Southeast Asia, about three weeks ago. It was a fourteen-hour flight each way, and my ear felt blocked with a lot of popping the whole way home.
Doctor: Any pain in the ear or drainage?
Patient: No pain, no drainage. No ringing either, and I haven't been dizzy.
Doctor: Did you swim or put anything in your ears while you were away?
Patient: I swam a couple of times in the hotel pool. I use cotton swabs every day. And I took pseudoephedrine 60 mg three times a day for the stuffy nose on the flights.
Doctor: Okay. Anything going on with your eyes?
Patient: Yes, both eyes have been itchy and red since I got back, with watery tearing. No eye pain, and my vision is the same as always.
Doctor: Any fever or sore throat?
Patient: No fever. Just the stuffy nose.
Doctor: Any medical problems or allergies to medicines?
Patient: Seasonal allergies, that's all. No drug allergies.
Doctor: Alright. Your vitals today are blood pressure 126/78, heart rate 72, and temperature 98.4. Looking in the right ear, there is a plug of wax against the drum. The left canal is clear and the left drum looks normal. We did a wax removal with a curette today, and afterward the right drum is intact and a little retracted, with no fluid and no redness. Inside your nose the lining is pale and boggy. Both eyes show mild redness of the white part with no discharge, the corneas are clear, and your vision is 20/20 in each eye.
Patient: Is the hearing loss from the wax?
Doctor: Mostly. The audiogram we did before you came in shows a mild conductive loss on the right and a normal result on the left, and tympanometry shows reduced movement of the right drum. So my impression is cerumen impaction with eustachian tube dysfunction from your allergies and the flights, plus allergic conjunctivitis.
Patient: What should I do?
Doctor: Stop the cotton swabs and stop the pseudoephedrine. Start fluticasone nasal spray, two sprays in each nostril once a day. Start olopatadine 0.1 percent eye drops, one drop in each eye twice a day. We will repeat the hearing test in six weeks, and come back sooner if you get ear pain, drainage, or a sudden change in your hearing.
Patient: Sounds good, thank you.
summary: A 48-year-old male presented with four months of gradual right-sided muffled hearing that worsened after a long international trip, along with itchy red eyes and a stuffy nose. He denied ear pain, drainage, ringing, dizziness and fever. Exam showed cerumen impaction on the right, a pale boggy nasal lining and mild conjunctival redness, and the audiogram showed a mild right conductive loss. The impression was cerumen impaction with eustachian tube dysfunction and allergic conjunctivitis, treated with wax removal. He was told to stop cotton swabs and pseudoephedrine, start fluticasone nasal spray and olopatadine eye drops, and repeat the hearing test in six weeks.

Rheumatology clinic follow-up. This 37-year-old male returns for follow-up of ankylosing spondylitis, diagnosed three years ago after MRI of the sacroiliac joints showed sacroiliitis and he tested positive for HLA-B27. He reports persistent inflammatory low back pain that wakes him in the second half of the night, with morning stiffness lasting about 45 minutes that improves with exercise. He takes naproxen 500 mg twice daily with only partial relief. He denies eye redness or eye pain, denies abdominal pain or black stools, and denies swelling of his peripheral joints. He has no other medical problems and takes no other medications.

On examination, blood pressure was 124/78 and heart rate 70. He has tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, a modified Schober test of 3 cm, and chest expansion of 3 cm. There is no peripheral synovitis and no heel tenderness. His CRP today is 14 mg/L, mildly elevated, and his BASDAI score is 5.2, which indicates active disease despite an adequate NSAID trial.

Impression: ankylosing spondylitis with persistent moderate disease activity on an NSAID. I discussed options and we agreed to start adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks once screening is complete. He will continue naproxen 500 mg twice daily. I ordered QuantiFERON-TB testing and hepatitis B serologies before the first dose, and referred him to physical therapy for a spine mobility program. Follow-up in 3 months.

The impression was persistently active ankylosing spondylitis on an NSAID. Telehealth video visit, infectious disease. Patient is a 23-year-old male connecting from home on a smartphone video call. Patient identity and location confirmed verbally.

Reason for visit: painful rash on the right side of the trunk.

History (patient-reported): Three days ago he noticed burning, tingling pain on the right flank, and the next day a rash appeared in a band wrapping from the middle of his back around to the right upper abdomen. The pain is 6 out of 10 and worse at night. He denies fever, chills, headache, and any rash on the face or around the eyes. He has no vision changes and no weakness. He had chickenpox as a child. He takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies. He works rotating warehouse shifts, including overnight shifts, so his sleep and meal times vary from day to day.

Home measurements: temperature 98.6 F with a home thermometer.

Visual exam by video: clustered vesicles on an erythematous base in a single band on the right flank, confined to one side of the midline, with a few new vesicles near the edge and no crusting yet. No lesions on the face, neck, or scalp. He is comfortable, speaking in full sentences, and appears well.

Clinical impression: herpes zoster, thoracic dermatome, within the 72-hour window for antiviral therapy.

Management: Start valacyclovir 1000 mg three times daily for 7 days. Acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain. I advised him to set phone alarms so doses are spaced evenly across his shift days, to keep the rash covered, wash hands often, and avoid contact with newborns, immunocompromised people, and anyone who has never had chickenpox or the vaccine until the lesions crust. Call or be seen in person for fever, spreading rash, eye involvement, or worsening pain. Video follow-up in 1 week.

Doctor: Good afternoon. Thank you for coming in. I have a professional interpreter on the line today, so I will speak in short sentences and pause so everything can be translated. I have you down as a 20-year-old female here for follow-up of your rheumatoid arthritis. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. My hands are still hurting a lot, mostly in the morning.
Doctor: How long does the stiffness last in the morning?
Patient: Maybe one hour and a half. My fingers are swollen and it is hard to make a fist. My wrists hurt too.
Doctor: Any fever, mouth sores, cough, or trouble breathing?
Patient: No fever. No sores in the mouth. No cough and no trouble breathing. My asthma has been calm.
Doctor: Good. Any nausea or vomiting after the methotrexate?
Patient: No nausea. No vomiting.
Doctor: Let's go through your medicines one by one, because I want to be sure. Tell me how you take the methotrexate.
Patient: I take four pills one time in the week.
Doctor: Please read me the label on the bottle you brought.
Patient: Hmm. It says methotrexate 2.5 mg, take six tablets by mouth once a week. Oh, sorry, it is six. Four was the old dose. I forgot the doctor changed it last time.
Doctor: Thank you for checking. Six tablets of 2.5 mg is 15 mg once a week. Do you ever take it on other days?
Patient: No, only one day each week, always the same day.
Doctor: Good. What about folic acid?
Patient: The small yellow pill, 1 mg, every day.
Doctor: And the prednisone?
Patient: Prednisone 20 milligram every morning.
Doctor: Please look at that label too.
Patient: It says prednisone 5 mg, take two tablets every morning. So that is ten. I am sorry, I said twenty by mistake.
Doctor: No problem. So the prednisone is 10 mg every morning, and that is the correct dose. What else do you take?
Patient: Ibuprofen 600 mg three times a day for the pain, from the pharmacy without a prescription. Iron pills, ferrous sulfate 325 mg once a day, for low blood. And the albuterol inhaler when I feel tight.
Doctor: Thank you. You take methotrexate, folic acid, prednisone, ibuprofen, iron, and albuterol. Do you use birth control?
Patient: Yes, the implant in my arm.
Doctor: Good, because methotrexate can harm a pregnancy. Your urine pregnancy test today was negative.
Doctor: Now your numbers. Blood pressure 108/68, heart rate 78, temperature 98.2, oxygen saturation 99 percent. On exam you have 6 tender joints and 4 swollen joints, mostly the knuckles and wrists of both hands. Your lungs are clear, there are no mouth ulcers, and I see no rash or nodules. Your blood tests from last week show WBC 5.6, hemoglobin 11.2, platelets 310, ALT 24, creatinine 0.7, and CRP 18, which is mildly high.
Patient: Is the medicine working?
Doctor: Partly. My impression is that your rheumatoid arthritis is still moderately active. Your asthma is stable, and your iron deficiency anemia is mild. The blood tests show the methotrexate is safe for your liver, kidneys, and blood counts, so I want to increase the methotrexate from 15 mg to 20 mg once a week. That is eight tablets of 2.5 mg, all on the same day, one day a week. Keep taking folic acid 1 mg every day and prednisone 10 mg every morning.
Patient: What about the ibuprofen?
Doctor: Please stop the ibuprofen. It can make asthma worse and it adds stomach and kidney risk with methotrexate. Continue the iron and the albuterol. I will repeat the CBC, liver tests, and creatinine in 4 weeks, and I want to see you again in 6 weeks.
Doctor: To be sure I explained clearly, can you tell me in your own words how you will take the methotrexate?
Patient: Eight tablets, one day each week, the same day. No ibuprofen.
Doctor: Exactly right. I will give you a picture schedule and a pill box labeled with the days. Call us right away for fever, mouth sores, cough, or trouble breathing.
summary: A 20-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis was seen with an interpreter for ongoing hand pain, swelling and 90 minutes of morning stiffness, with no fever, mouth sores, cough or nausea. Her medication doses were clarified with the bottle labels, confirming methotrexate 15 mg weekly and prednisone 10 mg daily. Exam showed 6 tender and 4 swollen joints, labs were safe and CRP was mildly high, and the impression was moderately active rheumatoid arthritis with stable asthma and mild iron deficiency anemia. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg once a week, ibuprofen was stopped, other medicines continue, and repeat labs are planned in 4 weeks with follow-up in 6 weeks.

Dictating a follow-up visit in the oncology clinic. The patient is a 38-year-old male with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma, never smoker, PD-L1 expression 80 percent, no actionable driver mutation, on pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks. Today is cycle five, correction, cycle six. His wife attends today and provides part of the history because he tends to minimize his symptoms.

Per the patient he feels more tired over the past 3 weeks, and he is cold all the time even when others are comfortable. His wife adds that he has been sleeping about 12 hours a night, has gained some weight, and has had constipation, which is new. He reports a mild dry cough that is unchanged since starting treatment. He denies fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, diarrhea, abdominal pain, rash, and headache. His wife agrees that he has had no vomiting or blood in the stool. Appetite is good. His only other medication is acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for mild back discomfort, which he rarely uses.

Vital signs today: blood pressure 122/76, heart rate 56, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air, temperature 98.2 F. Weight is up 3 kg from the last cycle. On exam he is in no distress and ECOG performance status is 1. His skin is dry. The thyroid is not enlarged or tender. Lungs are clear with no wheeze. Abdomen is soft and nontender. No peripheral edema.

Data. TSH is elevated at 14.2, free T4 is low at 0.6, and his baseline TSH before starting immunotherapy was 2.1. White count 6.8, hemoglobin 12.9, creatinine 0.9, ALT 31. Restaging CT chest last week showed a partial response of the primary tumor and no new lesions.

Assessment. One, stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with partial response on pembrolizumab. Two, immune-related hypothyroidism, which explains the fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, and low heart rate. Three, mild dry cough, stable, with no signs of pneumonitis.

Plan. Proceed with pembrolizumab cycle six today. Start levothyroxine 50 mcg daily on an empty stomach, and I reviewed this with both the patient and his wife. Repeat TSH and free T4 in 6 weeks. Wife counseled to call for new shortness of breath, diarrhea, or severe fatigue. Return in 3 weeks for the next cycle.

The assessment was immune-related hypothyroidism with a responding lung cancer. Cycle six of pembrolizumab proceeds, levothyroxine 50 mcg daily was started, TSH and free T4 will be rechecked in 6 weeks, and he returns in 3 weeks.

Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 63-year-old female here for follow-up of your breast cancer. How have you been doing on the anastrozole?
Patient: Overall okay, but my joints are so stiff. My hands and knees ache, especially in the morning, and it has gotten worse since I started it about eight months ago.
Doctor: How bad is the aching, and does it keep you from doing things?
Patient: About a five out of ten. It takes me half an hour to loosen up, and I have been walking less because of my knees.
Doctor: Any swelling or redness in the joints?
Patient: No swelling, no redness.
Doctor: Any hot flashes?
Patient: A few at night, nothing terrible.
Doctor: Any new lumps in the breast or armpit, or changes in the skin or nipple?
Patient: No lumps, no changes.
Doctor: Any bone pain, back pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, or vaginal bleeding?
Patient: No to all of those.
Doctor: What medicines are you taking?
Patient: Anastrozole 1 mg once a day, amlodipine 5 mg for my blood pressure, and Tylenol sometimes for the aches.
Doctor: Do you take calcium or vitamin D?
Patient: No, I don't.
Doctor: Okay. Your vitals today are blood pressure 134/82 and heart rate 76. On exam, both breasts and both armpits are free of masses, the scar from your surgery is well healed, and I feel no enlarged lymph nodes. The knuckles and both knees are mildly tender without swelling or warmth. Your mammogram last month was normal. The bone density scan you had last week shows a T-score of -2.7 at the hip, which is osteoporosis.
Patient: Is the cancer back?
Doctor: No. There is no sign of recurrence. You had an ER-positive breast cancer treated with lumpectomy and radiation 18 months ago, and the mammogram is clear. The joint aches are from the anastrozole, and the anastrozole can also thin the bones, which is why the scan shows osteoporosis.
Patient: What do we do about it?
Doctor: Continue the anastrozole once a day, because it lowers the chance of the cancer returning. Start alendronate 70 mg once a week, first thing in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, and stay upright for 30 minutes. The patient is a 65-year-old male with resistant hypertension, type 2 diabetes, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, and hyperlipidemia who was admitted with hypertensive urgency. Interval events. No acute events overnight. His blood pressure on arrival was 192/108 and it has improved to 148/86 on oral medications. He denies headache, palpitations, episodic sweating, and flank pain today. He has not noticed easy bruising, muscle weakness, or recent weight gain. He works as a warehouse supervisor on rotating night shifts, so his sleep and meals are irregular and he often sleeps only 4 to 5 hours.

Medications. Lisinopril 20 mg daily, correction, lisinopril 40 mg daily, confirmed with the outpatient pharmacy. Amlodipine was increased this admission from 5 mg to 10 mg daily. Spironolactone 25 mg daily was started by his primary doctor two months ago and has been discontinued because potassium was 5.4 on admission. Metformin 1000 mg twice daily. Atorvastatin 40 mg at bedtime. He received dexamethasone 1 mg by mouth at 11 PM last night for the overnight suppression test.

Vital signs: blood pressure 148/86, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, temperature 98.5 F. On exam he is obese with central adiposity, but there are no purple striae, no moon facies, no dorsocervical fat pad, and no proximal muscle weakness. Heart is regular, lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema.

Data review. CT abdomen shows a 3.2 cm homogeneous left adrenal nodule with unenhanced attenuation of 8 Hounsfield units, consistent with a lipid-rich adenoma. The right adrenal gland is normal. Plasma free metanephrines are normal, so pheochromocytoma is ruled out. The overnight dexamethasone suppression test gave an 8 AM cortisol of 3.1 mcg/dL, which is in the indeterminate range. Two, indeterminate dexamethasone suppression, so autonomous cortisol secretion has not been excluded, and the shift work makes cortisol rhythm testing unreliable. No further adrenal imaging is needed given the 8 Hounsfield unit attenuation. Continue lisinopril 40 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, metformin, and atorvastatin, and do not restart spironolactone. Endocrine clinic follow-up in 6 weeks, scheduled on a day off from his shifts.

Patient is a 71-year-old female, at home. Identity confirmed with two identifiers and she consented to a phone visit. No video, so no visual exam was possible; findings below are patient-reported.

Reason for visit: right hand numbness and tingling, carpal tunnel syndrome follow-up.

History: Six months of numbness and tingling in the right thumb, index, and middle fingers that wakes her two to three times a night. Shaking the hand relieves it. It is worse when she holds her phone or drives. She drops cups and has trouble with buttons. She denies neck pain, pain radiating from the shoulder or elbow, tingling in the left hand, and fever. She has had no recent injury. Her arm does not feel weak overall. The hand feels clumsy.

She works as a home health aide with rotating day and overnight shifts, so her sleep times change week to week and she often forgets or cannot use her night splint when her sleep is in the daytime.

Nerve conduction study ordered by her primary doctor two months ago showed moderate right median neuropathy at the wrist and a normal left side. Past history: hypertension and hypothyroidism, TSH normal last month. Medications: amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, and over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg two or three times a day for hand pain. No known drug allergies.

Home measurements: blood pressure 132/78 and pulse 70 on her home cuff.

Guided self-exam by phone: holding her wrists flexed for 60 seconds brought on tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers within 30 seconds. Tapping over the wrist at home also reproduced the tingling. She reports she can make a full fist and touch her thumb to each fingertip. Speech was clear and she was comfortable on the call.

Impression: right carpal tunnel syndrome, moderate by nerve conduction study, with night symptoms and mild loss of hand function. Blood pressure is acceptable on home readings.

Management: Stop the ibuprofen because of her age and blood pressure. Start acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed, maximum 3000 mg a day. Wear a neutral wrist splint whenever she sleeps, whether that is day or night, and during repetitive tasks. Schedule an in-person visit within 2 weeks, on a day off from work, for a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel. If symptoms return or weakness develops, I will refer her for surgical carpal tunnel release. Take breaks from repetitive wrist flexion at work. Continue amlodipine and levothyroxine. Call sooner for constant numbness or loss of grip strength.
